sections.heading: When darkness exposes what is in me
sections.text: Sovereign Lord, when dark thoughts, unbelief, and a practical godlessness rise up in me, help me not to treat it as random or harmless. Show me your loving purpose even in this painful exposure. If I have leaned on old spiritual victories as if they made me safe, correct me. If I have taken your Spirit’s comfort for granted, teach me to treasure him more. Heal the hidden places in me where I can live as if you were not real, not near, and not worthy of my trust.
theological_themes: God can use seasons of spiritual darkness and conviction as fatherly discipline, not to destroy his child but to expose pride and deepen dependence.
The Spirit’s comfort is a gift to be treasured, and its felt absence can reveal how much the believer depends on God’s mercy.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents God’s discipline as the loving work of a Father who trains his children for holiness. It supports the prayer’s request to see even painful conviction and humbling as part of God’s good purpose.
David asks God to search him and expose any grievous way in him. That matches the prayer’s desire for God to uncover hidden godlessness rather than leave it untreated.

sections.heading: Teaching me to come down from my pride
sections.text: Teach me to humble myself before you. Let me see how empty human praise is when it starts to stand between you and me. Let me want your will more than I want the feeling of spiritual success—even when your will is to withhold comfort instead of give it. Show me the truth about my own heart: that apart from you my thoughts, words, and actions are hollow and bent toward evil. When you allow me to feel the pull of sin, and even the pressure of the enemy, use it to make me honest, lowly, watchful, and stronger in dependence on you. And when unbelief closes my eyes to your majesty, power, mercy, and love, open them again.
theological_themes: Humility includes seeing the emptiness of human honor, submitting to God’s will, and honestly recognizing the corruption of the heart apart from grace.
God may permit temptation and inward struggle to expose sin and drive the believer into greater dependence, vigilance, and strength in him.

scripture_references.connection: James calls believers to humble themselves before God, resist the devil, and draw near to the Lord. This directly supports the prayer’s movement from pride and temptation toward lowliness and renewed nearness to God.
Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. That grounds the prayer’s confession that the heart, mind, speech, and life are empty without God’s life and help.
The father’s cry, asking Jesus to help his unbelief, gives biblical language for the believer who both trusts and feels the real obstruction of unbelief.

sections.heading: Asking you to take full possession of me
sections.text: So take hold of me again, Lord. Fill the space my pride and unbelief have tried to occupy. You alone are good. You alone are worthy. I do not want a self-directed life with religious words around it. I want to belong to you completely.
theological_themes: God alone is truly good and worthy of full allegiance.
Repentance is not only turning away from sin but yielding oneself back to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers, in view of God’s mercy, to present themselves to God as a living sacrifice. This supports the prayer’s desire to be wholly possessed by God rather than ruled by self.
The psalmist confesses that God is his supreme desire and portion. That illuminates the prayer’s claim that God alone is good and worthy.

sections.heading: Remembering that sin is never a small thing
sections.text: Do not let me treat sin lightly. You are not pretending when you convict me. Satan is not pretending when he tempts me. And I am not pretending when I sink under the weight of what I have done and what I am. Sin is not a game, not a harmless habit, not a small thing to manage. Keep me from forgetting that the deepest evil of sin is not only what I did, but whom I sinned against: you, the holy and living God.
theological_themes: Conviction, temptation, and sin are spiritually serious realities, not trivial matters.
The gravity of sin is measured especially by the holiness and greatness of the God against whom it is committed.

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession recognizes that sin, even when it harms others, is ultimately against God. This directly grounds the prayer’s emphasis that sin’s deepest seriousness lies in the greatness of the One offended.

Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief. This supports the prayer’s desire for conviction that is serious, truthful, and spiritually fruitful rather than shallow remorse.
Peter warns believers to be sober-minded because the devil actively seeks to devour. This reinforces the prayer’s refusal to treat temptation as imaginary or harmless.

sections.heading: Finding comfort in Christ when I fear what is ahead
sections.text: When I am afraid of what may come, steady me with the truth. In myself, I am weak, dying, and guilty before you. But in Christ, I am reconciled to you, made alive, and given what my soul needs. In myself, I have no strength to do anything truly good. But in him, you give me what I need to endure, obey, and serve. What I have now in Christ is real, but it is still only a beginning. Soon I will have it fully, with you, where sin, fear, weakness, and darkness are gone forever.
theological_themes: The believer’s hope is not in self-improvement but in union with Christ: reconciliation, new life, strength, and final glory.
Christian assurance holds together present possession in Christ and future perfection in heaven.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says believers who were once enemies are reconciled to God through Christ and now rejoice in that reconciliation. This supports the prayer’s comfort that, though guilty in oneself, the believer is brought near in Christ.
This passage describes God making sinners alive with Christ by grace. It grounds the prayer’s contrast between being spiritually dead in oneself and alive in Christ.
In context, Paul speaks of Christ strengthening him to endure all circumstances. This supports the prayer’s confidence that weakness is met by Christ’s enabling strength.
Peter points believers to a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven. This fits the prayer’s already-and-not-yet hope: what is possessed now in Christ will be received fully in the life to come.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original speaks of God 'withdrawing the Spirit.' In a modern evangelical setting, this could be heard as the Spirit abandoning a believer, which would conflict with the doctrine of the Spirit’s abiding indwelling. I rendered it as the felt loss of the Spirit’s comfort and help, while preserving the original idea of God using spiritual dryness to humble and teach.

The original says sin and Satan are 'allowed power' in the believer. I preserved the providential and spiritual-warfare emphasis, but phrased it carefully so God is not presented as morally causing sin. The adaptation speaks of God permitting the believer to feel temptation and the pull of sin for humbling and dependence.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'atheism' in the original not as formal intellectual atheism only, but as practical godlessness in the heart—living or thinking as if God were absent or unworthy of trust.

I retained the original’s severe language about the self—guilty, weak, dying, and unable to do good apart from Christ—because that is central to the prayer’s penitential force, but paired it closely with the original’s comfort in reconciliation, new life, and future perfection in Christ.

I rendered 'spiritual enjoyments' as the experience of spiritual comfort and success, since the original appears to refer to felt consolation and vitality in communion with God rather than mere emotional pleasure.
